note: Every way a generated page may point INSIDE a file, and what it means. Written by hand, per webview/conformance/README.md: a vector is a claim about behaviour, and generating it from one implementation would only prove that implementation agrees with itself. The page side (scripts/webview-location) and the host side (webview-core) both assert against this file.
grammar: A fragment is the part after '#' in a link, without the '#'. One leading '#' is tolerated and stripped.
'L<line>' and 'L<from>-L<to>' are explicit positions and always win.
'<ref>' names a region or a declaration, with inject-examples' scope modifiers '-' (body only), '+' (with annotations) and '++' (with annotations and the doc comment).
In a .json file the reference is a comma-separated list of dotted key paths, because JSON has no comments to hang a region on.
A bare name is a declaration in a source file, and a heading anchor in a document (.md, .markdown, .html, .htm) - which is why a link to '#install' in a README is left to the page itself.
Anything else is not a location and stays an ordinary link.

cases.why: the maintainer's example: a method inside a source file
an explicit line, the spelling the JetBrains host resolves today
a range, which the host selects rather than a caret
a one-line range is still a range: the page asked for a selection
line 0 means the first line rather than an error, per the contract's clamp rule
a reversed range is a page's mistake; the grammar reports what was written and the host normalises
an open-ended range is not a location
a leading '#' is tolerated, because a page has the fragment either way
a declaration or a region, by bare name
the body only, without the signature
the declaration and its annotations
the declaration, annotations and doc comment - the form the resolver docs use
three plus signs is malformed, not a region called '+add'
two minus signs is malformed, not a region called '-add'
regions exist in every file type, markdown included
in .json the reference is the JSON rule: one dotted key path
and the JSON rule takes a list, which is why the two rules are told apart by the file's type
whitespace around the keys is the writer's formatting, not part of a key
an array element is a dotted path like any other

a bare fragment in a document is a candidate too: the page scrolls to a heading of that name without asking anyone, and only asks a host when the name is not one - which is how a README region link works
and the same is true of HTML, whose anchors are its own
but an explicit line in a document is still a location
a nested or qualified declaration name is a member like any other
a scheme-like fragment is not a location; a colon is never part of a reference
a declaration needs a file type to be told from a heading anchor, so no path means no member
an explicit position needs no file type at all
and neither is an empty fragment: the file itself, which needs no navigation

THE maintainer's case: a bare name spelled like a region, with no prefix at all - it is a name exactly like a method or a field, and what it resolves to is the host's business (a declaration, or a #region directive of that name)
a declaration name and a region name are the same reference: a link should not have to know which one the author wrote
a scope modifier needs no prefix either - no language here has a declaration whose name starts with a minus, so it is unambiguous
the same, with the bare plus form
and the bare double plus, the form the resolver docs use
a modifier with nothing after it names nothing
three minuses is not a modifier, and not a name either
in .json there are no declarations to find, so a bare reference is the JSON rule: dotted key paths
including the list form, without the prefix
and in a document a region works the same way bare: the prefix is never required, only allowed
in .json a bare reference is the JSON rule before any modifier rule: JSON has no regions, and a leading dash is a legal key character
